tone_statements.quote: 2.3 Tones Kana can be analysed as having four contrastive tones, as follows; Ikoro (1996) Orthographic Example Gloss High ˊ ˊ fá intestine Rising ᷇ ̈ fä vehicle Mid ˉ unmarked fa x weeded Low ˋ ˋ fà to weed The convention of using a diaeresis for the rising tone is not very helpful, as it easily become confusing in some contexts, especially on 'i'. I am therefore considering replacing it in due course.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger & Kay Williamson. 2008. The Ogoni languages: comparative word list and historical reconstructions. Ms., Cambridge/rogerblench.info.
sources.note: Comparative wordlist with a phonology preamble for the Ogoni group; may state the prosodic type of Kana and cites the Kana phonology literature.

sources.citation: Bond, Oliver & Gregory D. S. Anderson. 2005. Divergent structure in Ogonoid languages. Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 31(2), Special Session on Languages of West Africa, pp. 13-24. doi:10.3765/bls.v31i2.818
sources.note: Silent on stress. Section 1 'Phonology and Lexis' and 2.1 'Coda restrictions' treat phonotactics only; the only prosodic remark is tonal: 'Noun class prefixes in Ogonoid, when present, usually carry a low tone, or else the tone is copied from the initial syllable of the root. Data from Kana shows that this is merely a tendency.. (Ikoro 1996:58)' (p. 14). No word 'stress' or 'accent' anywhere in the Ogonoid text.

sources.quote: 2.3 Tones Kana can be analysed as having four contrastive tones, as follows; Ikoro (1996) Orthographic Example Gloss High ˊ ˊ fá intestine Rising ᷇ ̈ fä vehicle Mid ˉ unmarked fa x weeded Low ˋ ˋ fà to weed The convention of using a diaeresis for the rising tone is not very helpful, as it easily become confusing in some contexts, especially on 'i'. sources.locator: §2.3 Tones, p. 4; preface p. 2 for the remark on tone-marking conventions
sources.note: The phonology preamble has a section 2.3 'Tones' stating that Kana can be analysed as having four contrastive tones (High, Rising, Mid, Low) with a minimal quadruplet on fa and a concordance of Ikoro's (1996) tone marks vs the dictionary's orthographic marks; the preface adds that the ms. tone-marking conventions differ from Ikoro (1996) and contain a sporadic circumflex 'not matchable to existing tone analyses'; entries are tone-marked throughout. No statement on stress.

sources.note: The only full descriptive grammar of Kana (PhD Leiden); WALS, Grambank and Bond & Anderson all code from it. Its phonology chapter (tone system, syllable structure) is where a stress/accent statement or an explicit 'tone language, no stress' statement would sit. HathiTrust holds it search-only, so a librarian full-text search for 'stress' would at least give page hits.
